opus-5.5.text:
I think the most promising path is making simulation much easier to build, not only faster to run.

For decades the field has focused on better numerical methods: more accurate integrators, better discretizations, more robust solvers. That work still matters a lot. But in my experience the real bottleneck is often the cost of turning an idea into working, high-performance code. A researcher might have a great idea for a new material model or a new coupling scheme, and then spend months fighting with GPU kernels, memory layouts, sparse data structures and parallelization bugs. Many good ideas never get tested because the engineering cost is too high.

So the direction I'm most excited about is better programming abstractions: languages and compilers that let you write simulation code close to how you think about the physics, while the system handles performance. That was the motivation behind Taichi. If you can separate *what* you want to compute from *how* it is laid out in memory and scheduled on hardware, people can iterate ten times faster. Iteration speed is what drives progress.

The second direction is **differentiable simulation** and its connection with machine learning. Once your simulator is differentiable, it becomes more than a forward tool for predicting what happens. You can use gradients to optimize controllers, infer physical parameters from observations, design shapes, and train neural networks with physics in the loop. I don't think neural networks will simply replace numerical simulation, because physics gives you structure, guarantees and generalization that pure data-driven models struggle with. But combining the two, with learned components where the physics is unknown or too expensive and classical solvers where we understand things well, is very powerful.

Third is hardware. GPUs and other accelerators keep evolving, and simulation methods should be co-designed with them. Some algorithms that looked inefficient on CPUs become very attractive on massively parallel hardware, and the reverse is also true.

To sum up: make simulation **productive**, make it **differentiable**, and make it **hardware-aware**. If we do those three things well, many more people, including artists, engineers and roboticists as well as numerical analysts, will be able to use simulation creatively. That broader participation is how the field moves forward fastest.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies engineering effort as a bottleneck, while saying numerical-method work still matters; it does not say progress in purely numerical simulation has reached a bottleneck.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes differentiable simulation’s connection to machine learning as powerful, but names making simulation easier to build as the most promising path.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss elastoplasticity models or argue that data-driven models could outperform them.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the most promising path is making simulation programmable by far more people than it is today. For a long time, high-performance physical simulation has been locked behind a wall: you need to know the physics, but you also need to know CUDA, memory layouts, sparse data structures, and how to squeeze a GPU. Most researchers who understand the physics don't have time to become systems engineers, so a lot of great ideas never get implemented efficiently.

That's really what drove the design of Taichi. The idea was to let someone write code that looks like simple Python, loops over particles or grid cells, and have the compiler worry about parallelization, vectorization, and data layout. When you decouple the algorithm from the way data is laid out in memory, you can try a dense grid, a sparse grid, or a hash table without rewriting the whole program. That turns out to be a huge productivity multiplier. A graduate student can go from an idea to a GPU-accelerated prototype in an afternoon instead of a month.

The second piece I'm excited about is differentiability. Once a simulator is written in a language that can automatically generate gradients, simulation stops being just a forward tool for rendering or prediction. It becomes something you can optimize through. You can fit material parameters to real footage, do inverse design, or embed physics inside a learning pipeline. The combination of fast, differentiable, and accessible is where I think a lot of new work will come from.

And finally, I think the community matters as much as the technology. If the tools are open and approachable, people in graphics, robotics, computational physics, and even education start sharing code and building on each other. That cross-pollination is how the field moves faster than any single lab can push it.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most promising directions is to rethink simulation algorithms and the programming systems behind them together. A better numerical method is important, but so is making that method easy to implement, experiment with, and run efficiently on parallel hardware.

There’s also a lot of opportunity in differentiable simulation. Usually, we specify a system and simulate what happens. If we can differentiate through that simulation, we can work backward: given a desired outcome, how should we change the design or the control inputs? That makes simulation useful not just for predicting behavior, but for optimizing it.

For me, the exciting path is bringing those pieces together—numerical methods, efficient computation, and tools that let more people explore new ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one promising direction is to make numerical simulation easier to program and faster to run. There’s often a gap between describing a physical model mathematically and implementing it efficiently on modern hardware. If we can reduce that gap, researchers can spend more time exploring ideas and less time optimizing code.

Another exciting direction is combining simulation with machine learning. Simulation brings physical structure, while learning can help with parts that are difficult to model or expensive to compute. The challenge is to get that benefit while preserving the accuracy and reliability we need.
